Precious Metals Quarterly 2009 Q4 

# Executive summary 

## Platinum market deficits: 2011-14 

The platinum market should begin a period of gradual normalisation from 2010, after its 2009 dislocation. 

We expect the physical market to return to a period of sustained deficits from 2011 for the first time since the early 2000s, peaking at 510,000oz in 2012, before approaching a more finely balanced market towards the end of our forecast period. A rise in net fabrication demand will be supported by increasing momentum in the automotive and industrial sectors as the world economy turns. But delayed investment means that miners, who have been forced to prioritise cost management and cash preservation, will find it difficult to meet this increase in industrial consumption, even as total mine supply moves back towards its 2006 peak. 

We expect the internal combustion engine to remain the dominant vehicle propulsion technology over our forecast period; consequently the automotive sector will remain a major source of platinum demand. The heavy duty diesel sector for on-road and non-road vehicles and engines will offer significant expansion opportunities for platinum-rich after-treatment systems, as will the increased take-up of fuel efficient light duty diesel and hybrid vehicles in mature markets. We also expect autocatalyst-related platinum demand from developing economies to exceed demand from North America and Japan for the first time, reflecting strong production growth in light duty petrol vehicles fitted with autocatalyst devices.  In the jewellery sector, China will remain a key and growing platinum market, despite a pullback in net offtake. 

We expect prices in real terms to consolidate around $1,400/oz over our forecast period - not enough to accelerate significant new mine supply. Price support will come from a tightening physical market as well as investment-related demand for hard assets. In 2009 H2, investor interest in platinum-related investment vehicles strengthened, reflecting a greater investor willingness to assume cyclical exposure in the form of industrial metals as the risk of a ‘W’ shaped global recovery receded and uncertainty about the economic and fiscal impact of US reflationary policies persisted.  Although there will undoubtedly be some close out of positions ahead of the end of the calendar year, particularly those taken on margin, we expect investmentrelated demand for platinum to continue in 2010 and to remain a price support over the remainder of our forecast period. Investor demand for platinum will reflect ongoing uncertainty about the direction of the US dollar and the reaction of financial markets to policy makers’ attempts to exit extraordinary monetary and fiscal stimulus. Although ETF net flows will continue to influence short term price movements to some extent, we would not be surprised if liquidation of platinum ETF holdings proves stickier than in the past.

ecious Metals Quarterly 2009 Q4 Executive Summary ## Other precious metal markets ### Gold We take the view that re-monetisation of gold, at the national and international level, will now be a dominant driver of the gold price. - We have raised our gold price forecasts, particularly for 2012-14, and expect nominal gold prices to remain mostly above $1,100/oz - Whether or not gold is included in any recomposed IMF SDR basket in late 2010 (it could be deferred to the next review in 2015) will set the scene for what subsequently happens to the gold price. - The sharp rise in bullion prices has led to an increase in actual and potential mine supply but consumers outside China have capped budgets for jewellery purchases. ### Silver Our forecast annual market balances through to 2014 develop in much the same manner as we were projecting three months ago. However, we have raised our short-term price forecast. - Mine supply has run only a little short of our last projection, and firm plans remain in place that will result in another significant year of growth in 2010. - We continue to project demand falling by approximately 10% this year, but now believe that it could recover all of its losses since 2000 within the next five years. - Market’s surpluses will be greatest in 2009-10, but stocks will still rise to at least the equivalent of 1.8 years of fabrication demand. ### Palladium We still expect the palladium market to remain in fundamental surplus over our entire forecast period, but these surpluses ought to narrow from 1.1 million oz in 2009 to 0.2 million oz by 2014. - Although surpluses will be higher than we had previously estimated, when adjusted for the possibility of less pronounced Russian state destocking, physical metal availability could be less abundant than in previous years. - This tightening of the physical market combined with investment-related demand for hard assets should support the price. We have revised up our palladium price forecasts, to reflect developments in the physical market, as well as in the wider precious metals complex (particularly gold). From this base, our forecast for the next five years can be described broadly as consolidation around $390/oz in real terms - Announcements in the last quarter confirm that a number of operations, currently on care and maintenance, are due to restart in 2010: Lac des Iles in Canada and Everest in South Africa. ## Data sources and study team 

The historical data presented in this report are based on estimates published by a variety of sources, including Johnson Matthey (JM), World Gold Council (WGC), International Financial Statistics (IFS), JD Power, London Bullion Market Association (LBMA), World Bureau of Metal Statistics (WBMS), CPM, GTIS trade statistics, company websites and written reports. 

However, CRU’s interpretation of the data may or may not coincide with those expressed in these various sources. 

The forecast is exclusively CRU’s.
